blocks.text: Quillon Harbor Advisors
How we came to this work

Quillon Harbor began with an observation about the companies we knew best: industrial and business-services firms, built over decades by the people who still owned them, that tended to come to market with less advice than their size and their history deserved. The larger banks were not organized to give a business of that scale their full attention, and the smaller brokers were not equipped to run the kind of process that gets an owner a fair price on fair terms.

We set out to run sell-side processes for those owners the way a larger firm would run them, with a properly researched buyer list, marketing materials written to survive a buyer's diligence, and a disciplined sequence from first contact to signed agreement. What we meant to keep, and have kept, is the senior attention an owner is entitled to when the business on the table is, in most respects, the work of a lifetime.

The buy-side work followed from the sell-side work. Private-equity sponsors who had met us across the table in a sale began to ask whether we would search a sector on their behalf, screening a long universe of candidates down to the few worth approaching, and we found that the habits that serve a seller serve a buyer just as well. From time to time a board also asks us for a fairness opinion, and we accept that work only where we can give an independent read with no stake in the outcome.
What that history asks of us now

Because we learned the business by advising owners, we explain each stage of a process before it begins, and we are careful never to promise in a letter what the process itself cannot deliver. Heather Delacruz, our Managing Partner, reads every engagement letter and every fairness opinion before it leaves the office, and she holds all of us to the habit of telling a client plainly what happens next.

Our deal teams are small on purpose, and the same few names stay with a mandate from the first meeting to the closing. Underneath each team sits analytical work we would be content to put in front of any board: David Rios, an Analyst in our advisory practice, builds the target screens and comparable-transaction tables our teams lean on, and every figure in them carries its source and its denominator.

On a buy-side search the same care takes the form of a record. A sponsor working with us can see why each candidate in the universe was kept or set aside, how many survived each screen and on what criteria, and which conversations moved a company forward or took it off the list.

Continuity of that kind does not happen by accident. Cynthia White, our Chief of Staff, keeps the operating rhythm of the firm, from the pipeline meeting to the staffing grid that records who is on which mandate, so that an owner never discovers halfway through a sale that the people advising them have changed.

Confidentiality, for us, is less a policy than a way of writing. In anything that circulates, a target is described by its sector and its revenue band and is named only in documents that are already privileged, a discipline our clients notice early and, we think, come to value.
An example from this year's work

Of the mandates we are able to describe in a document of this kind, our sell-side engagement for {{fact:f:E-2014-001.client}} gives a fair picture of how we work: a small and settled team, a process set out for the client stage by stage before it began, and analytical material built to be read as closely by a buyer's diligence team as by our own.

We offer it as one illustration among the engagements we are carrying this year, not as a catalogue of the practice, and its particulars remain, as every client's do, between the firm and the people who engaged us. Much of the work we do in any year cannot be named in a document like this one at all, which is as it should be.

An owner weighing a sale, or a sponsor with a sector in mind, should begin with a conversation with Heather Delacruz, who will set out in that first meeting how a process with us would run and what we would need to see before we could advise on it.

Melissa Jacobson has joined Quillon Harbor as an Analyst in the advisory practice, and it is a real pleasure to welcome her. She reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and because we are still a small firm in which analysts work on live mandates from the outset, she will be drafting material for real owners well before she has learned where every file is kept. The industry sections of our sell-side books will be her first charge, and since they are the part of a book a generalist buyer reads first, the work matters more than its place in the binder suggests.

blocks.text: Melissa's first review will come after her first few months with us, and it will be a conversation about her writing as much as about her research. Mark Allen will go through a handful of her drafts with her, an industry overview among them, and talk plainly about what reads well, what needs tightening and where a generalist buyer would lose the thread. Heather Delacruz reads the early written work of every new analyst as well, so that the firm's standard is applied to everyone in the same way.

Before then, the one thing we ask is that Melissa bring her first industry overview to Mark in draft, however rough, so that the two of them can shape it together before it goes anywhere near a client.

Justin Gonzalez's first morning at Quillon Harbor began the way every new arrival's does, with Heather Delacruz walking him through how the firm writes, which matters here as much as how it models. He joins the advisory practice as an Analyst, and we are very glad to have him: a firm that is asked for careful valuation work needs someone who enjoys the arithmetic, and Justin plainly does. We have asked the deal teams to bring him into their conversations early, so that he hears how a number is used before he is asked to produce one.

Justin's work will center on valuation: the trading comparables and precedent-transaction sets that sit beneath a sell-side pricing discussion, and the football-field summaries a partner carries into a boardroom when a board has asked us for an independent read. He reports to Mark Allen, Partner, who will decide which mandates he joins and will review his models before any figure leaves the building. Within the practice he sits with the other analysts, whose buyer lists and target screens his numbers will often need to agree with, and he will learn quickly that a comparable set is only as good as the reasoning behind each company in it.

For his first months we are asking for accuracy and explanation before speed. Every comparable set should show its sources and the date its prices were taken, every adjustment should be one he can defend aloud in a sentence, and every model should go to Mark with a short note on what Justin would want a second person to check, a habit we hope he keeps long after he needs it.

None of this is meant to hold him back for long, and we expect his work to be in use on live mandates early on. The first piece of work on his desk is the comparables set for a current sell-side mandate, and Mark will sit down with him to go through it as soon as a first draft is done.

Amanda Thomas joins Quillon Harbor as our Compliance Manager, working within Operations, and she reports to Cynthia White, Chief of Staff. The conflict checks, the confidentiality logs and the careful wording of anything that touches a regulated question are now her particular charge, which means that before long nearly every mandate in the firm will pass across her desk at least once, and we are glad that it will.

A read-through of the conflicts log with Cynthia White, mandate by mandate, including the checks still open.

An introduction to the confidentiality log and the rule behind it: targets are described by sector and revenue band in anything that circulates, and named only where the document is already privileged.

Separate conversations with each of the partners about how their current mandates are staffed and papered.

blocks.text: For day-to-day questions, and for anything touching staffing or the firm's calendar, Amanda should go first to Cynthia White, who keeps the staffing grid that shows who is on which mandate and is usually the quickest route to an answer. A question about a particular engagement, its parties or its paper is best taken to the partner leading that mandate. Anything that bears on what the firm says in a letter or an opinion, or on what it is prepared to promise, can come to me, Heather Delacruz, directly.
Her first task, once the week's introductions are done, is a short written note to Cynthia setting out any gaps she finds in the conflicts log, which we will use to decide what to put right first.

Everyone at Quillon Harbor joins Heather Delacruz in welcoming Kelly Brown, who has come to the advisory practice as an Analyst. Kelly has already shown, in her first conversations here, a habit of asking good questions and asking them in writing, and we hope she keeps it.

Kelly's work will sit on the buyer side of our sell-side processes: building the list of prospective acquirers for each mandate, keeping the contact log once outreach begins, and following each party from the first call through a signed NDA to whatever indication it eventually submits. She reports to Mark Allen, Partner, who will decide which mandates she joins first. On each process she will work inside a small deal team that quotes her counts to a client and needs them to be right every time they are quoted, and she will find that the same few names recur across a mandate from its first week to its last.

In her first months we will ask her for completeness and sourcing above everything else, so that every name on a buyer list has a stated reason for being there and every entry in a contact log records who spoke to whom, when, and about what. We would also ask her to go on putting her questions in writing, numbered at the foot of an email if she likes, since a question set down that way tends to get a properly considered answer. Because a contact log names parties that no circulating document ever would, it lives only in the privileged folder for its mandate, and a copy found anywhere else is a mistake to be put right at once.
The first piece of work on her desk is the buyer list for a current sell-side mandate, and she will take Mark Allen through it as soon as a first draft is ready.

We are very glad to welcome Angela Cole, who joins the advisory practice as an Analyst. She reports to Mark Allen, Partner, and most of her time will go to our buy-side search programs, where a sponsor's criteria meet a long universe of candidate companies and someone has to narrow the one against the other with care, and leave a record of how it was done. Her notes on a screen should read as an audit trail of that narrowing, marking which figures are estimates and which came from a conversation, and the table below sets out what she will carry and with whom.

blocks.text: Angela's first review will be tied to a piece of work and not to a date on the calendar. Once she has carried one screen from the full universe down to a shortlist, Mark Allen will go through her screening log with her line by line, ask her to reproduce two or three of the counts from the underlying data, and talk through what she would do differently a second time. A short written note of that conversation will go in her file.
Her first assignment is the initial screen for a current buy-side program, and Mark will brief her on the sponsor's criteria before she begins.
